items.reference: Thanks for calling. I understand your internet's been dropping intermittently over the past few days. Before we dig in, let me confirm a few things about your setup. You're on our Fibre 500 plan, is that right? And the modem is the one we shipped in September — the black one with three green lights on the front. Good. First, I'd like you to look at those lights right now. Are all three of them solid green, or is any of them blinking, off, or a different colour? Okay, so the middle light is amber. That's actually really helpful — amber on the middle indicator means the modem is reaching the local exchange but not receiving a stable authentication response. That points to something in our network rather than in your home, which is good news for you. Let me check the line status from my end. I'm seeing three brief drops in the last twenty-four hours, each lasting between forty seconds and two minutes. That matches what you described. There's a scheduled maintenance window that ran on your exchange overnight — the drops are consistent with the recovery pattern after that kind of work. I'm going to flag this to network engineering as a post-maintenance stability issue and open a ticket in your name. Reference number is going to be TS-4482-91. You should see stability return within twelve to twenty-four hours.

items.reference: The Moon is slowly moving away from the Earth at a rate of about 3.8 centimetres per year. This is due to tidal interactions: the same forces that create ocean tides transfer angular momentum from the Earth's rotation to the Moon's orbit.

items.reference: Good evening. I'm Sarah Chen, and this is the 6 o'clock news. Our top story tonight: the government has announced an emergency package worth 14 billion pounds to help households and businesses with rising energy costs. The Chancellor confirmed the measures in a statement to Parliament this afternoon, saying the package would take effect from the 1st of May. Under the plan, households will receive a flat payment of 400 pounds, with additional support for the lowest-income families of up to 650 pounds. Businesses in the hospitality, retail, and manufacturing sectors will receive rebates on their energy bills for a period of six months. The announcement was welcomed by opposition leaders, though the shadow chancellor called it too little too late, pointing out that average household bills have risen by 67 percent over the past 18 months. Industry groups broadly welcomed the support but said longer-term solutions were still needed. The cost of the package will be funded partly through a windfall tax on energy companies, which the government is extending for a further two years. Several energy firms said they would review planned investment in domestic production following the announcement. We'll have more on this story throughout the evening. Now let's go to our economics correspondent James Okafor, who is outside the Treasury.

items.reference: Thanks for calling. I understand your internet's been dropping intermittently over the past few days. Before we dig in, let me confirm a few things about your setup. You're on our Fibre 500 plan, is that right? And the modem is the one we shipped in September — the black one with three green lights on the front. Good. First, I'd like you to look at those lights right now. Are all three of them solid green, or is any of them blinking, off, or a different colour? Okay, so the middle light is amber. That's actually really helpful — amber on the middle indicator means the modem is reaching the local exchange but not receiving a stable authentication response. That points to something in our network rather than in your home, which is good news for you. Let me check the line status from my end. I'm seeing three brief drops in the last twenty-four hours, each lasting between forty seconds and two minutes. That matches what you described. There's a scheduled maintenance window that ran on your exchange overnight — the drops are consistent with the recovery pattern after that kind of work. I'm going to flag this to network engineering as a post-maintenance stability issue and open a ticket in your name. Reference number is going to be TS-4482-91. You should see stability return within twelve to twenty-four hours.

items.reference: The Moon is slowly moving away from the Earth at a rate of about 3.8 centimetres per year. This is due to tidal interactions: the same forces that create ocean tides transfer angular momentum from the Earth's rotation to the Moon's orbit.

items.reference: Good evening. I'm Sarah Chen, and this is the 6 o'clock news. Our top story tonight: the government has announced an emergency package worth 14 billion pounds to help households and businesses with rising energy costs. The Chancellor confirmed the measures in a statement to Parliament this afternoon, saying the package would take effect from the 1st of May. Under the plan, households will receive a flat payment of 400 pounds, with additional support for the lowest-income families of up to 650 pounds. Businesses in the hospitality, retail, and manufacturing sectors will receive rebates on their energy bills for a period of six months. The announcement was welcomed by opposition leaders, though the shadow chancellor called it too little too late, pointing out that average household bills have risen by 67 percent over the past 18 months. Industry groups broadly welcomed the support but said longer-term solutions were still needed. The cost of the package will be funded partly through a windfall tax on energy companies, which the government is extending for a further two years. Several energy firms said they would review planned investment in domestic production following the announcement. We'll have more on this story throughout the evening. Now let's go to our economics correspondent James Okafor, who is outside the Treasury.

items.reference: Good evening. I'm Sarah Chen, and this is the 6 o'clock news. Our top story tonight: the government has announced an emergency package worth 14 billion pounds to help households and businesses with rising energy costs. The Chancellor confirmed the measures in a statement to Parliament this afternoon, saying the package would take effect from the 1st of May. Under the plan, households will receive a flat payment of 400 pounds, with additional support for the lowest-income families of up to 650 pounds. Businesses in the hospitality, retail, and manufacturing sectors will receive rebates on their energy bills for a period of six months. The announcement was welcomed by opposition leaders, though the shadow chancellor called it too little too late, pointing out that average household bills have risen by 67 percent over the past 18 months. Industry groups broadly welcomed the support but said longer-term solutions were still needed. The cost of the package will be funded partly through a windfall tax on energy companies, which the government is extending for a further two years. Several energy firms said they would review planned investment in domestic production following the announcement. We'll have more on this story throughout the evening. Now let's go to our economics correspondent James Okafor, who is outside the Treasury.

items.reference: The Moon is slowly moving away from the Earth at a rate of about 3.8 centimetres per year. This is due to tidal interactions: the same forces that create ocean tides transfer angular momentum from the Earth's rotation to the Moon's orbit.

items.reference: Good evening. I'm Sarah Chen, and this is the 6 o'clock news. Our top story tonight: the government has announced an emergency package worth 14 billion pounds to help households and businesses with rising energy costs. The Chancellor confirmed the measures in a statement to Parliament this afternoon, saying the package would take effect from the 1st of May. Under the plan, households will receive a flat payment of 400 pounds, with additional support for the lowest-income families of up to 650 pounds. Businesses in the hospitality, retail, and manufacturing sectors will receive rebates on their energy bills for a period of six months. The announcement was welcomed by opposition leaders, though the shadow chancellor called it too little too late, pointing out that average household bills have risen by 67 percent over the past 18 months. Industry groups broadly welcomed the support but said longer-term solutions were still needed. The cost of the package will be funded partly through a windfall tax on energy companies, which the government is extending for a further two years. Several energy firms said they would review planned investment in domestic production following the announcement. We'll have more on this story throughout the evening. Now let's go to our economics correspondent James Okafor, who is outside the Treasury.

items.reference: Thanks for calling. I understand your internet's been dropping intermittently over the past few days. Before we dig in, let me confirm a few things about your setup. You're on our Fibre 500 plan, is that right? And the modem is the one we shipped in September — the black one with three green lights on the front. Good. First, I'd like you to look at those lights right now. Are all three of them solid green, or is any of them blinking, off, or a different colour? Okay, so the middle light is amber. That's actually really helpful — amber on the middle indicator means the modem is reaching the local exchange but not receiving a stable authentication response. That points to something in our network rather than in your home, which is good news for you. Let me check the line status from my end. I'm seeing three brief drops in the last twenty-four hours, each lasting between forty seconds and two minutes. That matches what you described. There's a scheduled maintenance window that ran on your exchange overnight — the drops are consistent with the recovery pattern after that kind of work. I'm going to flag this to network engineering as a post-maintenance stability issue and open a ticket in your name. Reference number is going to be TS-4482-91. You should see stability return within twelve to twenty-four hours.

items.reference: Good evening. I'm Sarah Chen, and this is the 6 o'clock news. Our top story tonight: the government has announced an emergency package worth 14 billion pounds to help households and businesses with rising energy costs. The Chancellor confirmed the measures in a statement to Parliament this afternoon, saying the package would take effect from the 1st of May. Under the plan, households will receive a flat payment of 400 pounds, with additional support for the lowest-income families of up to 650 pounds. Businesses in the hospitality, retail, and manufacturing sectors will receive rebates on their energy bills for a period of six months. The announcement was welcomed by opposition leaders, though the shadow chancellor called it too little too late, pointing out that average household bills have risen by 67 percent over the past 18 months. Industry groups broadly welcomed the support but said longer-term solutions were still needed. The cost of the package will be funded partly through a windfall tax on energy companies, which the government is extending for a further two years. Several energy firms said they would review planned investment in domestic production following the announcement. We'll have more on this story throughout the evening. items.reference: Good evening. I'm Sarah Chen, and this is the 6 o'clock news. Our top story tonight: the government has announced an emergency package worth 14 billion pounds to help households and businesses with rising energy costs. The Chancellor confirmed the measures in a statement to Parliament this afternoon, saying the package would take effect from the 1st of May. Under the plan, households will receive a flat payment of 400 pounds, with additional support for the lowest-income families of up to 650 pounds. Businesses in the hospitality, retail, and manufacturing sectors will receive rebates on their energy bills for a period of six months. The announcement was welcomed by opposition leaders, though the shadow chancellor called it too little too late, pointing out that average household bills have risen by 67 percent over the past 18 months. Industry groups broadly welcomed the support but said longer-term solutions were still needed. The cost of the package will be funded partly through a windfall tax on energy companies, which the government is extending for a further two years. Several energy firms said they would review planned investment in domestic production following the announcement. We'll have more on this story throughout the evening. Now let's go to our economics correspondent James Okafor, who is outside the Treasury.

items.reference: Thanks for calling. I understand your internet's been dropping intermittently over the past few days. Before we dig in, let me confirm a few things about your setup. You're on our Fibre 500 plan, is that right? And the modem is the one we shipped in September — the black one with three green lights on the front. Good. First, I'd like you to look at those lights right now. Are all three of them solid green, or is any of them blinking, off, or a different colour? Okay, so the middle light is amber. That's actually really helpful — amber on the middle indicator means the modem is reaching the local exchange but not receiving a stable authentication response. That points to something in our network rather than in your home, which is good news for you. Let me check the line status from my end. I'm seeing three brief drops in the last twenty-four hours, each lasting between forty seconds and two minutes. That matches what you described. There's a scheduled maintenance window that ran on your exchange overnight — the drops are consistent with the recovery pattern after that kind of work. I'm going to flag this to network engineering as a post-maintenance stability issue and open a ticket in your name. Reference number is going to be TS-4482-91. You should see stability return within twelve to twenty-four hours.

items.reference: Good evening. I'm Sarah Chen, and this is the 6 o'clock news. Our top story tonight: the government has announced an emergency package worth 14 billion pounds to help households and businesses with rising energy costs. The Chancellor confirmed the measures in a statement to Parliament this afternoon, saying the package would take effect from the 1st of May. Under the plan, households will receive a flat payment of 400 pounds, with additional support for the lowest-income families of up to 650 pounds. Businesses in the hospitality, retail, and manufacturing sectors will receive rebates on their energy bills for a period of six months. The announcement was welcomed by opposition leaders, though the shadow chancellor called it too little too late, pointing out that average household bills have risen by 67 percent over the past 18 months. Industry groups broadly welcomed the support but said longer-term solutions were still needed. The cost of the package will be funded partly through a windfall tax on energy companies, which the government is extending for a further two years. You're on our Fibre 500 plan, is that right? And the modem is the one we shipped in September — the black one with three green lights on the front. Good. First, I'd like you to look at those lights right now. Are all three of them solid green, or is any of them blinking, off, or a different colour? Okay, so the middle light is amber. That's actually really helpful — amber on the middle indicator means the modem is reaching the local exchange but not receiving a stable authentication response. That points to something in our network rather than in your home, which is good news for you. Let me check the line status from my end. I'm seeing three brief drops in the last twenty-four hours, each lasting between forty seconds and two minutes. That matches what you described. There's a scheduled maintenance window that ran on your exchange overnight — the drops are consistent with the recovery pattern after that kind of work. I'm going to flag this to network engineering as a post-maintenance stability issue and open a ticket in your name. Reference number is going to be TS-4482-91. You should see stability return within twelve to twenty-four hours.

items.reference: Good evening. I'm Sarah Chen, and this is the 6 o'clock news. Our top story tonight: the government has announced an emergency package worth 14 billion pounds to help households and businesses with rising energy costs. The Chancellor confirmed the measures in a statement to Parliament this afternoon, saying the package would take effect from the 1st of May. Under the plan, households will receive a flat payment of 400 pounds, with additional support for the lowest-income families of up to 650 pounds. Businesses in the hospitality, retail, and manufacturing sectors will receive rebates on their energy bills for a period of six months. The announcement was welcomed by opposition leaders, though the shadow chancellor called it too little too late, pointing out that average household bills have risen by 67 percent over the past 18 months. Industry groups broadly welcomed the support but said longer-term solutions were still needed. The cost of the package will be funded partly through a windfall tax on energy companies, which the government is extending for a further two years. Several energy firms said they would review planned investment in domestic production following the announcement. We'll have more on this story throughout the evening. Now let's go to our economics correspondent James Okafor, who is outside the Treasury.

items.whisper: Good evening. I'm Sarah Chen, and this is the 6 o'clock news. Our top story tonight. The government has announced an emergency package worth £14 billion to help households and businesses with rising energy costs. The Chancellor confirmed the measures in a statement to Parliament this afternoon, saying the package would take effect from 1 May. Under the plan, households will receive a flat payment of £400, with additional support for the lowest-income families of up to £650. Businesses in the hospitality, retail, and manufacturing sectors will receive rebates on their energy bills for a period of six months. The announcement was welcomed by opposition leaders, though the shadow Chancellor called it too little too late, pointing out that average household bills have risen by 67% over the past 18 months. Industry groups broadly welcomed the support, but said longer-term solutions were still needed. The cost of the package will be funded partly through a windfall tax on energy companies, which the government is extending for a further two years. Several energy firms said they would review planned investment in domestic production for the next two years. following the announcement. We'll have more on this story throughout the evening. Now let's go to our economics correspondent, James Okafor, who is outside the Treasury.
